profile.campus: Helsinki, Finland (Equinix HE5, part of Equinix's Helsinki-region cluster)
profile.reading:
This is Equinix's HE5 facility at Sahamyllyntie 4B in Helsinki, Finland, part of a cluster of Equinix buildings, HE3 through HE7, that the company markets collectively under its Helsinki region heading. Equinix's own dedicated page describes HE5 as a two-story, reinforced-concrete building with 1,106 square meters, about 11,905 square feet, of colocation space, N+1 power and cooling redundancy including free-cooling capability, generator autonomy of 30 hours or more at full load, and a 99.9999%-plus global uptime guarantee, though it does not publish a specific IT capacity figure in megawatts or kilowatts. Equinix entered the European colocation market through its 2007 acquisition of IXEurope and expanded further through its 2015 acquisition of TelecityGroup for about $3.8 billion, though Equinix's current HE5 page does not attribute the building to either predecessor company by name. Equinix, founded in Silicon Valley in 1998 by former Digital Equipment Corporation facilities managers Al Avery and Jay Adelson, converted to a real estate investment trust in January 2015 and trades on Nasdaq as EQIX; the company's own about page states a current global footprint of 281 data centers across six continents, while Wikipedia separately cites approximately 260 data centers across 33 countries as of 2025.

As an EU-based facility, this data center falls under the European Union's Energy Efficiency Directive reporting requirements, which since 2024 have required data centers above a minimum capacity threshold to report power usage effectiveness, water usage, and other sustainability metrics to a European Commission database, part of a broader EU push for standardized data center energy transparency that does not have a direct equivalent in most of the US markets covered elsewhere in this registry.

reading.body:
Equinix HE5 in Helsinki is a 11,905-square-foot colocation facility with no published IT capacity figure, making its contribution to AI infrastructure compute footprint opaque despite EU regulatory requirements for energy transparency.

The facility operates as part of Equinix's five-building Helsinki cluster, which the company assembled through organic deployment and two major European acquisitions: IXEurope in 2007 and TelecityGroup in 2015 for $3.8 billion. Equinix's current marketing materials do not attribute HE5 to either predecessor company by name, obscuring the acquisition history that shaped European data center capacity. The building offers standard colocation tier features: N+1 redundancy, 30-hour generator autonomy, free-cooling capability, and a 99.9999%-plus uptime commitment.

The absence of published megawatt ratings is the limiting fact. Equinix's own facility page does not disclose IT load capacity in kilowatts or megawatts, preventing direct assessment of how much compute this building can support or how it ranks within the regional cluster. This represents a gap between physical infrastructure (square footage, redundancy systems, location) and the resource that actually constrains AI: electrical power.

European data centers face stricter disclosure regimes than most US facilities. Since 2024, the EU Energy Efficiency Directive requires facilities above a capacity threshold to report power usage effectiveness, water consumption, and other metrics to the European Commission. These requirements create opportunities for standardized comparison across the EU market, though they do not automatically make data public.
